sentences.text: This meeting is being recorded.
Hi.
Hey, Aaron, how you doing?
I'm good, how are you?
Yeah, I'm good, thank you, I'm good.
Whereabouts are you calling from?
Good stuff.
We're in London, so just now Old Street.
Ah, brilliant.
How about you?
Well, I'm in Somerset but I know Old street very well.
Very nice.
Cool.
Enjoying the sunshine out in the middle of nowhere.
Yeah, yeah, it's nice, yeah.
I grew up in Devon so I kind of.
Yeah, I miss it.
Every now and again go down there and get a breath of fresh air.
But yeah, yeah, good stuff.
Ah, Devin's really nice as well.
Nice one.
Well, look, I've been interested in speaking to you for a while, so.
Interested to get.
Get your assigned NDA through.
I think I spoke to somebody else at your place last time there.
Is it Vishal?
Oh, possibly, yeah.
But yeah, all good.
So you've signed a few NDAs on Agencies Co, which is our platform.
It's probably.
I don't know how much you know about the rest of the business, but it's probably good to give you a quick overview and where you're at.
Yeah, so we are, we're capital A and we are an M and A advisory for marketing services companies.
So we work both on the buy and the sell side, but we have a marketplace, agencies co for.
For sellers, but also we work with buyers as well, helping them to find the targets for the types of agencies that they're looking to acquire.
So those could be marketing agencies, high growth or ambitious agencies or with private equity as well directly and investment teams.
So the good thing is we get to see both sides of the table and we know what offers look like, good ones and bad ones.
Um, but you guys are interested in making some acquisitions yourself?
Yeah, so yeah.
Be good to sort of learn a little bit more about what it is that you're trying to achieve and how we can help you do that.
Yeah, so I guess, I guess I'll give a bit of a background of.
Yeah, around.
So we.
When did you.
Did you speak to Vishal?
Did you say.
Was that recently?
Was that a while ago?
September 23rd.
So it's quite a while ago.
Okay, yeah.
Okay, cool.
I guess things have moved on a bit since then anyway.
So, yeah, we're.

Yeah, an agency, we're based in London, working mainly in the music industry and we also have an office in Medellin, Colombia, servicing the kind of Latin American clients which again is mostly mostly music space.
And then we have a software development team that.
That's kind of remote and yeah, building kind of tools and platforms internally.
So we have a kind of white labeled campaign management software which we've just started.
So we have internal campaign management software and we just started kind of licensing that out to some of our label clients.
And we, we have a kind of micro influencer tool which is a bit like.
So it's an automated campaign setup tool.
So you kind of, it's a bit like Facebook ads but for influencers.
So you put your budget, your targeting things, targeting requirements, run dates and then our tool kind of like automatically search through our platform.
Micro influencers send them brief and then we have a kind of approval, automated approval flow.
So it's very hands off again.
Yeah, so that's for sort of micro campaigns.
And then we have the kind of service part of the agency which is yeah running campaigns for our clients.
Guess the trends that we're seeing are a move amongst our clients into like in housing parts of this and centralizing their sort of influencer marketing strategies.
If you like kind of backtrack three years or so.
Labels weren't really structured.

Music engine wasn't really structured to be able to like handle the volume of payments, the volume of creators, just the, the pure like volume of work that was that that goes in, in running these campaigns effectively.
So the role of agencies in that instance is quite clear.

And over time labels are wanting to in house a lot of the strategy and manage these things and so they're a lot more keen to use tools and technologies and that's where we're seeing our role with them is going to be more of a kind of software rather than like a managed service.
So I guess what we're kind of looking to do is continue, continue kind of down that path.
And then we're also looking to expand the agency and, and look at new industries that we could kind of work within.
Kind of leveraging our music expertise and understanding of how trends form and working with micro influencers.
So we work, we work with about, we push out about 50,000 posts a year across yeah across our kind of range of tools which works out yeah about four or five thousand a month.
And so we can kind of handle like a huge scale and we're looking to work to leverage that to work with other industries.

So I guess where M and A comes into that we're looking at potentially looking at other agencies where we can kind of plug that are purely service that we can kind of leverage some of our tools and things that we've already built and open us up to kind of new Industries as opposed to going in completely cold into those places.

And there's a kind of the general trend that we see is around smaller influencers at scale and that's what all of our software and everything has been designed to do and that's been what the music industry has kind of demanded from these types of campaigns.

So I think we're in a really good position to be able to understand that and to be able to I think like uni lead a Unilever's CEO the other week kind of put out an article saying that they're increasing their influence to spend.
And the whole rationale of that is they want one kind of ambassador influencer in each tiny little town across all of the regions they operate in.
And so it's that kind of thing that we're.
Yeah, we're really well set, well placed to kind of run those sorts of campaigns and I think gives us an edge against some of the other agencies.
So yeah, we're just looking at yeah, M and A opportunities.
So other agencies that have got a foothold in, in other industries.
So outside of music that either don't have software developed or, or where we can kind of use some of our software and help run this type of campaign that they might not already be.
Be doing.
Okay, cool, that's interesting.
Do you mind me asking about the size of round whereabouts are you at the moment in terms of like team size and revenue?
So in terms of billing.
So that's like the total.
You know, if, if a client is giving us ten grand we take.
If it's a serviced.
If it's yeah, part of the services we, we take a 30 roughly 30 to 35 as our commission.
And then if it's the micro campaigns our revenue is sort of 55 on those ones.
So top line billings like last 12 months is about £8 million GBP.
Our revenue is about 40% of that.
So it's three, three and a half ish.
And then profit, non adjusted profit is, is about 7 between 7 and 800,000.
If you take out some of the, if we capitalize on the development cost it goes to about 1.1 adjusted EBITDA.
Okay.
You've been talking to your accountant about capitalizing the development costs.
Yeah.
Yes, yes.
Sir.
Sense.
Oh, sorry, you just cut out for a second there.
I missed that.
It only makes sense in certain situations.
So.
But anyway, let's leave it there for now.
So I mean that's quite interesting.
Are you being approached by buyers very often?
We've explored it a little bit and Yeah, I think while like we would.

Yeah, I think that that's ultimately probably the aim, but I think the offers that we had at the moment are like, I think we can take it a little bit further than, than, than where we're at in terms of some of the offers.
So I think unless it was something that was above the.
Yeah, there was like a kind of premium there, then we're just gonna, we'll just keep kind of growing just out.
Of interest and obviously only if you're comfortable.
But what, what is the multiple that you're getting that you've not, you've not taken them up on those offers?
I think.
Well, I guess it kind of comes down to like what is involved in that as well.
So we had one that was a kind of 55% stake with some money going into the business, some paying out the shareholders and, and then they were going to be very hands off.
They'd have the option to acquire the rest.
And.
Yeah, and that was at evaluation.
Well, that, yeah, they said between 15 to 18 million dollars was, was what they said.
And I think what was unattractive about that was just that they were going to be very hands off and kind of.
Yeah, it was, it was a, it was a, it was a company that was backed by a public company and they were trading a much higher multiple.
And so it's a kind of an arbitrage thing for them.
So yeah, I think if there was like something that was strategically like a great fit and we could kind of see how there was like value add beyond, just beyond cash, then, then that'd be interesting.
But yeah, that, that's, that was the last one that we kind of talked about.
But so I guess you're looking to what's.
So what's the ambition?
Is it you're looking to build for yourself?
You want to create something bigger and keep going?
Or are you looking to build because you understand arbitrage and you're, you're trying to get to a certain size that you can exit at.
I think a bit of, a bit of both is the, the agency part.
To be honest, the agency part has always been a kind of like a hedge against if the tech didn't like fully work.
So I think if, if the software.

Yeah, we've got kind of like a couple of clients in that space and if we can scale that, like, you know, we think we might be able to, then that will probably become by far the most valuable part of the kind of group, if that makes sense.
The agency's part.
It Feels a lot kind of safer.
And I guess they are more in the continuing to do what we're currently already doing.
And, and if there's.
Yeah.
If there's ways that we can kind of.
That we can integrate other agencies.

I guess it kind of comes down to what I don't really want to do personally is to work for a company for another like three or four years where, you know, if I was going to exit, I would probably want like a shorter kind of handover period, if that makes sense of.
Of remaining within the company.
So.
So that kind of a part of it as well.
I wouldn't want a situation where someone owns kind of half of it indefinitely without like much of a plan.
It just.
You end in like, in a kind of weird limbo space.
Valuation is really good that they gave you.
But yeah, I understand the other part of it is not ideal because once you sold that 55, you can't get rid of the rest.
So basically they are getting it for half price, but they also overacted the price a little bit, so they didn't really make it cheap for themselves.
But it definitely in a position where you can't exit it.
So it's kind of pointless unless you like money, in which case you could have taken the money.
Okay, so.
So you're looking to build basically for the long term.
You want to put something on the map that's.
That scales.
The problem with music, I guess, is it.
It's difficult to scale.
And music companies don't like to spend money on marketing, so their budgets are tiny.
Yeah, it's lots of little budgets.
Is.
Is the way that that works.
But it kind of, you know, prepares you quite well for other types of campaigns.
We've done probably maybe between 5 and 10% of.
Of the work we do is not music.
And it's a completely different cadence.
Right.
The team and everything.
It's like music is like you get brief today and it's going live on Friday brands.
You get an intro today for something that's going live at Christmas.
And it's a completely different like cadence and way of working.
We don't.
We're just not, you know, the team as we currently have it aren't set up to work those sorts of timelines.
And you know, we just need to.
Yeah, I think it will be easier for us to.

I mean, that's like one of the attractive parts of acquiring an agency that, you know, you have the team that's already in the flow of understanding how these clients work and it's A case of adding on our services into what they're already pitching.
That feels a lot more manageable than starting from the ground up and building a team from scratch.
Yeah, 100%.
That's definitely the better way to go.
Okay, cool.
So how can I help you best?

Are we, are you looking for more agencies that appear on our platform and making sure that you, you don't miss any or are you looking to sort of pull the trigger on finding a business or businesses as quickly as possible and you want to look at volume?
Because there's two ways we can help.

One is that obviously you're in our mailing list and we know you exist, we know what you're looking for and so we're going to come and knock on your door when we have certain types of sell side clients or can we work with you on the buy side where we know what you're looking for but you have us on a retained basis and we're bringing those deals to the table every week for you so that we can get an acquisition done in a much short space of time rather than waiting for serendipity and hoping that something lands that, that you're looking for.
Yeah, I think we.
So we've done a few or we've done two acquisitions up to this point.
So we did and they've both been sort of, I guess non standard you could say.

First one was an influencer company who kind of managed creators and that was a kind of friend that I'd known like since, since I started round and, and he was just tired and kind of wanted, wanted to kind of like pass it on to someone.
So it was.
So that was the first one we did and then we just acquired a software company before Christmas which was sort of the opposite.
It was.
So it's a tool called TCAT.
It's a, it's a SaaS product and we acquired that plus the team, so five person development team and that was from One Media IP which is a public company on AIM.
Yeah, you might come across them.
So kind of like opposite side.
That was again, that was no cash, that was just we acquired it for shares of Round and.
Yeah, and so that was obviously a much more kind of formal process that, that we went through to, to complete that.
We.
Yeah, at the moment this is something I guess like kind of exploratory phase.

So we've, I guess we finished that, that the TCAT deal finished in November and we've just been sort of getting, getting that up to speed and everything and starting to look at what the plans are for the rest of the year.
So I think probably too early to go and like pull the trigger on some sort of.
Yeah, some sort.
I think we would need to like figure out exactly what it is in a bit more detail that we're looking for.
And I guess what would be useful is to understand maybe the size types of agencies or the size or the kind of like general like market at the moment.
Like what, what are other agencies looking for is it.
And, and all of the other parts that I guess that, that are around it.
So like how common is it that the founding team are going to stay on?
What type of deal structures are they going to be looking at?
Is it going to be like all cash at close or combination of these things?

Like yeah, figure out a few like main points I guess that like deal structures that you find people kind of most into and then yeah, like understand I guess the size of the types of agencies that you're working with.

So yeah, I mean there is no one answer for that really in terms of who we work with on the sell side we're working with agencies doing up to about 15, 20 million but all the way down from you know, about 500k or so.
So small to sort of mid size on the sell side.
In terms of deal structure, again it's not really something that you can put your finger on.
As you can tell from your own experience somebody's giving you this.
I hate the type of deal that you've been offered.
Actually we have those four clients every so often and I don't know anybody that's accepted one of those types of deals.

So I mean and for me that's, yeah, I mean it's not a great, it's not a great type of deal because Even though it's 55% it's control of the business and you can't get out, you can't sell 45% to somebody else who's not interested.
So but we, we do tend to see a sort of standard structure of, of deals particularly because they're, they're more common in the larger buyers that we work with and also private equity as well.
So they, that tends to be the sort of range of valuations for average agency agencies is, is something like 4 to 6.
So most holding companies are looking to buy sort of between the 5 and 7 mark I would say and if they can buy at the bottom of that range then they will.

And they're looking to give 50% cash up front and then a three year earn out sometimes they will roll over some equity, private equity, do do this more often where they will roll over a 20% of the business into the holding company or the platform business and then they will buy 80% with 40% cash up front and 40% as part of an earn out.
But there is no kind of standard deal.
Everybody's offering their own kind of deal.
But I would say that's probably the more common one that we see is 50, 40 or 50% cash up front and the rest is an earn out and then some equity rolled over or not.
Okay.
And you have.
So and your company then has like a, just like a list of.
Oh yeah, yeah.
How does it work in terms of like the platform and the, the I guess working on both sides.
Is there.
Yeah.
Is that, can you do that?
Is there like conflict ever?
I'm trying to think of it.
Occasionally there is.

So it doesn't, it doesn't happen in practice, at least not to the point where we've ever had to negotiate with ourselves to get a deal done.
So how does it work?
Do we have a list?
We have 130,000 agencies in our CRM.
So we're in constant contact with them depending on, you know, keywords that match for whatever we're searching for.
And that's a good starting place for us.
Most, you know, most of our clients are looking for a certain type of thing and we're able to locate those types of businesses based on the keywords that they're looking to match.
But we're constantly adding to that.
Every client has some different, you know, differentiator of the, the sort of variables that they want.
You know, they might want bigger or smaller or more people or less people or, or about to go bust or healthy.
You know, there's always something else that our clients want.
I think the main thing that, that is a commonality is that we look for off market opportunities.
So what we're not looking to do is go to a bunch of brokers, including ourselves, and find stuff that's for sale.
You never want to really buy something that's for sale if you can help it, because it usually comes with a set of problems.
Not, not 100% of the time, but certainly at the lower end of the market there is.
You're more likely to come across problems because if they're looking to sell, then they've got a reason to sell.
Right.
So what we do with our clients is we go off market and that's where the real value add is of what we're bringing to the table.
Because if you go as round to a bunch of other agencies that are similar to round, some of those are going to feel like they can't communicate openly with you because you're a competitor.

So if you have an M and a team that is approaching what may be competitors in the market or similar agencies, we're able to extract huge amount of information from them and share that with our client at the right time.
But they're more comfortable with that cushion between the two businesses.
But also, like I said, we're going off market.
So if we don't find it in our database, we don't find enough or we exhaust those that list quickly, then we will go out on the search as well.

You know, if you have a particular type of influencer, I mean, you're not looking for influencer agencies in music, but say you were, you know, there's probably a very small list that we can access easily.
And we're going to have to go out and find other agencies that aren't easily, you know, targetable.
But what we do is we start those conversations.
You know, it's a more relaxing way of, of beginning the conversation because they're not kind of guarded from day one.
Yeah, yeah.
So that's what we're doing for our clients and that's what our clients find it difficult to do.
Also, it's a huge time sync.

They just want to talk to you because you are who you are.
So we have those initial conversations.

We're able to, you know, get initial info.

But a one pager that gives you an overview of the business.

You've got that information in front of you for that very first conversation as well.

Is stage one.

The, the nice thing about.
Well, the nice thing for us about being on the buy side and going off market is that a lot of the sellers, they.
They're not engaged with a.
With a banker.

Months.

I mean, we.

So.
So, yeah, definitely.

My team will follow up.
Probably Jack or Ahmed will follow up about the Paris content Agency.
Cool.
Awesome.
Cool.
Good to speak with you.
Nice to meet you.

Cheers.

summary.overview: The Exploratory business development meeting between Aaron and Andy Day focused on the potential acquisition strategy of Round, a company specializing in influencer marketing within the music industry, which currently generates £3.5 million in revenue and is considering multiple acquisition opportunities. Capital A, the M&A advisory firm, provided insights on market trends, typical deal structures, and their extensive database of agencies for off-market opportunities. The meeting outlined a strategic plan for Round to expand into new industries by leveraging micro-influencer campaign expertise, alongside a detailed discussion of the due diligence process and associated costs. Action items included Aaron determining his budget and criteria for target acquisitions while Andy planned to follow up on these discussions and the prospect of a French content creation agency.
summary.short_summary: Aaron and Andy Day met to discuss the acquisition strategy for Round, a company specializing in influencer marketing within the music industry, currently generating £3.5 million in revenue. Capital A, the M&A advisory firm, provided insights on market trends and typical deal structures, highlighting their database of 130,000 agencies for off-market opportunities. The meeting focused on Round's desire to leverage its expertise in micro-influencer campaigns for expansion into new industries. They also discussed the due diligence process and costs associated with acquisitions. Action items included Aaron determining his budget and acquisition criteria, while Andy planned to follow up on a potential French content creation agency.
